en: Preface to Chan Master Xuzhou’s Commentary on the *Verses on the Regulations of the Eight Consciousnesses*:
The nature (*xing*) is one alone. Yet why speak of characteristics (*xiang*)? Nature is internal; characteristics are external.

If we do not speak of characteristics as external objects, but rather as the internal consciousness, then characteristics are also internal. External objects may impinge upon it, yet it remains unmoved—vast and open.

To take emptiness as one's refuge is still relatively easy to entrust oneself to; however, that which is retained within consciousness flows in subtle currents, such that its arising goes beyond the reach of cognition.
Even after reaching profound realization, one often laments the difficulty of eliminating habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and the fact that the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) has not yet been severed.

Those who study the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) must not fail to examine these words. Yet, those who speak exclusively of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) often pursue the superficial branches and rush toward the periphery.
Their efforts are exhausted in calculating grains of sand, or they are driven to despair by poring over paper.

Why do they not consider that when the ancients composed the treatises on Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*), they asked whether these various characteristics ought to exist or ought not to exist? Whatever exists...
All characteristics are empty and false. If one seeks the signless (*animitta*), should one seek it within characteristics, or rather seek it within the nature (*dharmatā*)?

If one seeks it within characteristics, there are the hundred dharmas arising from the eight consciousnesses; if one seeks it within the nature, the eight consciousnesses are transformed into the four wisdoms (*jñāna*).
Those in the world who pursue characteristics mostly fail, yet those who see the nature have never transgressed the characteristics.
They inquire about it and act upon it; once they have mastered it, they divide it into factions and contend over it, and in the end, it cannot be stopped—this is truly a cause for deep lamentation.
Master Xuzhou was a successor of Fuyan, yet he continued to study the scriptures of the Exoteric Teachings with great diligence.

Taking the "Verses on the Eight Consciousnesses" by the Tang Dynasty Master Xuanzang, he specifically composed a commentary upon them. The characteristics described in his commentary are not different from those of others, yet he draws them forth and...
I have brought this forth so that it ultimately returns to one’s inherent nature, enabling readers to attain awakening and realization. It is easy for Shi Zi to practice and a joy for Xu Zi to read;
thus, I had it beautifully carved into printing blocks to circulate it. Alas, will it not be of great benefit?
Ten days after the Dragon Boat Festival in the eleventh year of the Kangxi era. Written by Ju Li Wang Ting.
Preface to the Commentary on the Verses on the Eight Consciousnesses:

Formerly, the Venerable Ānanda, out of his compassionate heart, desired that people would understand that the triple world is mind-only and all phenomena are consciousness-only; he therefore composed the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* elucidates the Dharma-gate of the Characteristics School (*lakṣaṇavāda*). Its text is extensive and its meaning profound.

Later, Vasubandhu, fearing that students of the final age would find it difficult to grasp its essential points, compiled the texts of the *Yogācāra* and composed the *Triṃśikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Treatise in Thirty Verses on Consciousness-Only).
After this treatise was completed, masters such as Dharmapāla each produced their own commentaries based on their respective insights to explain this work. At that time...
The accumulated volumes and stacked fascicles were so voluminous that they could not be easily mastered.
Dharma Master Xuanzang, together with several other masters, condensed the most refined expressions and principles into ten fascicles, titled *Cheng weishi* (Establishing Consciousness-Only).

Later, Dharma Master Kuiji, seeing that students found it difficult to grasp the essential tenets of the ten-fascicle *Cheng weishi*, requested Master Xuanzang to compile these key points concerning the eight consciousnesses.

It is divided into four stanzas, each consisting of twelve lines. The fifty-one mental factors (*caitta*) are each assigned to their respective primary consciousnesses (*mūlavijñāna*) in an orderly and systematic fashion;
hence it is called "The Rules" (*Gomayapada*). Although the treatise consists of ten fascicles, its essential meaning is fully contained within these forty-eight lines.
By clarifying these few lines, I have raised the guiding framework of Master Xuanzang’s work with my own hand. Heaven [blessed this].

Have you not already gathered all those who are close to Maitreya within a single net? As for those who clarify even these few phrases, each school has its own point of awakening, which is certainly not lacking;

yet this remains their particular "gate" (men-t'ing). How many are there who can take form and return it to nature, and through awakening transform consciousness—like the Layman Lu, who knew that the five, eight, six, and seven consciousnesses undergo transformation as either fruit or cause, and that it is merely the transformation of names and words, devoid of any real nature?
Ah! When I first read Lu’an’s *Supplementary Commentary* and later examined Han-shan’s *General Exposition*, I could not help but admire their lofty insights.

However, if one wishes to transcend the mind, intellect, and consciousness to investigate the Way, and to sever the paths of ordinary beings and sages, how can the fifty-three stages of the Southern Journey avoid being surpassed by Maitreya’s final snap of his fingers? Therefore, true attainment lies in this very realization.
Regarding power: to exert less effort is to gain power. Those who merely explain do not desire its depth, but rather its shallowness;
that one proceeds from the shallow to the deep is the business of the awakened, not the business of the explainer.
Leaving My Staff at West Lake for Retirement: By the Recluse Xuzhou Shengdao.

Regarding the "Brief Explanation of the Rules of the Eight Consciousnesses," I have observed that the Master Xuanzang of the Tang dynasty possessed innate roots from his youth. For the sake of the Dharma, he crossed the shifting sands of the Taklamakan, undaunted by hardships and perils, until he encountered the transformation [of the Buddha].
Shen Manzhou was bestowed with the Dharma-seal; when he passed away, he could not be found—indeed, he could not be found.
Speaking in his natural colors, he sat away with ease. Is this not the one decisive stroke of his entire life? To produce a single translation is to manifest the Great Dharma to others.
Thus, reading these several dozen works closely, they are not only archaic and elegant, but truly possess the "eye on the crown of the head."
Illuminating all eight directions simultaneously, one is thus able to gather the myriad dharmas within the eight consciousnesses and transform those eight consciousnesses into the four wisdoms.
This causes the nature of consciousness to become brilliantly clear, like a fire in a cave or eyebrows drawn in a mirror.

By leading sentient beings from within the fields of their eight consciousnesses to realize the Great Samādhi of the Vajra, is not this milk of the Dharma exceedingly profound? Therefore, I have explained it through a simple exposition, rather than being bound by rigid formal instruction.

This is the practice of following the words (zixunxing). It is similar to the introductory expositions found in various other works; its sole purpose is to enable the reader to realize the underlying meaning beyond the mere pen and tongue.

Thus, it is yet another skillful means for those who seek awakening through cognition. If one persists in the notion of a self or clings to a sense of self-awareness, then every word becomes a source of affliction, and one instead establishes artificial boundaries between essence and characteristics (xingxiang). This was not the intention of Master Xuanzang, nor is it my own intention.
Regarding consciousness, it is categorized as the eight consciousnesses; I, however, maintain that in its totality, it is but a single consciousness.
It is simply that while the essence of consciousness is one, its functions are distinct. This is like the moon in the sky, which is but one, yet appears differently when reflected in various waters.

Therefore, those who now seek to awaken to consciousness wish to realize the essence through its functions; thus, what was originally a single pure brilliance becomes divided into six harmonious manifestations.
[They] merge; there is no separate entity. How, then, can their functions differ? For instance, visual consciousness and tactile consciousness are ultimately distinct;

thus, the five consciousnesses are strictly self-differentiated. As for that which is fully endowed with the fifty-one mental factors (*caitta*) and performs clear discernment, this definitely belongs to the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
However, it cannot maintain [the body]. As for that which is firm, persistent, and immovable—this is the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

The [consciousness] that definitely belongs to the seven consciousnesses cannot maintain seeds; as for that which contains and preserves [seeds] over many kalpas, it definitely belongs to the eighth consciousness.
The self-nature of these consciousnesses is such that they cannot be confused with one another. How could their essence be identical?

Furthermore, while the discrimination of the visual consciousness belongs to the eye, that which performs clear and distinct discrimination already pertains to the sixth consciousness of discrimination.
The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is its differentiation and firm grasping; it has already permeated the seventh consciousness’s clinging and maintaining.
The eighth consciousness’s containing and storing is its differentiation and non-forgetting; this nature of consciousness is inherently unified and admits no separation.
If practitioners merely recognize its functions, names and forms will be manifold; if they awaken to its essence, it is perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna*).

As for intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), intrinsic nature does not exist. This is why Master Xuanzang, at the beginning of each section on consciousness, first describes the delusions of its mental factors (*caitta*) and immediately follows with their untainted (*anāsrava*) state upon awakening. When one is deluded, there is no such awakening;
when one awakens, there is no such delusion. Thus, every consciousness is the wondrous function of the Self (*ātman*).
There are those who take the eight consciousnesses as the unconditioned essence (*asamskṛta-svabhāva*), positing the sixth consciousness alone as the mind-king (*citta-rāja*).

They liken this to a grinding stone, while the first five and the latter two [the seventh and eighth] serve as the mind-king’s assistants. This is because the first five consciousnesses respond to their respective sense organs and perceive their objects;

being all of the same type of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), they are devoid of both good and evil. As for the seventh consciousness, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "The seventh consciousness... [text fragment].

The cycle of transmigration is not the cause of birth and death. As for the eight consciousnesses, their essence is empty and quiescent; they are neither good nor evil, and are collectively categorized as indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

It is only the sixth consciousness, together with the preceding five consciousnesses, that induces the latter two consciousnesses and constitutes the very seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness.

Thus, through a single delusion, the three modes of cognition manifest, whereby the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) and the object-specific factors (*viśeṣabhūmika*) run rampant within the breast. One...
When one awakens and realizes that the three natures are empty, the causes and effects of outflows are, at that very moment, quiescent. Thus it is said:
"The sixth and seventh consciousnesses transform within the causal stage; the fifth and eighth are perfected upon the fruition. How profound these words!

For by taking the cause to encompass the fruition, one may, through the sixth consciousness alone, awaken deeply and immediately ascend to the ground of enlightenment. Yet, as for the perfect and clear knowledge of those of old, it did not require the exhaustion of the sense faculties.

Furthermore, why must one necessarily be hindered by these six consciousnesses when practicing the gates of contemplation? Thus, to believe in the six [consciousnesses] while disbelieving the eight is to fall into the biased attachments of the Two Vehicles.

There are those who take the eighth consciousness as the master of birth and death. This is because the nature of consciousness is rootless; when the root arises, the branches and leaves flourish together.

All other consciousnesses belong entirely to this [eighth consciousness], arising in their respective locations and ceasing in their respective locations; they are not capable of receiving perfuming or maintaining seeds.
Therefore, all other consciousnesses are coarse, whereas that which flows subtly and continuously is the eighth consciousness. All other consciousnesses are subsequent.

That which constitutes this initial false perception is the eight consciousnesses. One must understand that these eight consciousnesses are, in essence, the very first moment of non-awakening (abodhi) throughout immeasurable kalpas.
From this, one grasps at consciousness to form the sense organs, and grasps at the organs to receive sensory objects;

thus, one becomes entangled by the body, the sense organs, and the physical world, causing ignorance to flourish. This applies regardless of whether one is an ordinary person deluded regarding these consciousnesses or one who falsely clings [to them].
The provisional self of the five aggregates is a point at which even the intelligent non-Buddhists are deluded;

they speculate and cling to a divine self, thereby undergoing the suffering of birth and death within the realm of limited duration (*paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa*). Furthermore, those who advance to the two vehicles have not yet destroyed the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*);

and even Bodhisattvas prior to the seventh stage have not yet abandoned the innate clinging to a self (*sahaja-ātma-grāha*), whereby they undergo the birth and death of transformation (*pariṇāmi-jāti-maraṇa*).
This is a slight suffering. It is because they have all failed to achieve a great awakening regarding the most subtle aspect of the eight consciousnesses.

Therefore, within the gate of awakening, one must directly awaken until not a single thought arises; then the past and future limits are severed, and one will no longer fall into the error of a self coming first or going last, or entering and leaving a room.
The eight consciousnesses each lack a substantial nature; they all mutually serve as causes and conditions, arising through the deluded perceptions of sentient beings.
Thus, the first five consciousnesses interpenetrate the latter two, the seventh and eighth, and conversely, the seventh and eighth interpenetrate the first five.

This is like the head and tail of a Changshan serpent responding to one another, or like the beads on a rosary turning together to the left and right. If the first five consciousnesses did not exist, [the others] would ultimately not exist either.
Regarding what is seen: by whom is it clearly perceived? If there were no faculty of mind (*manas*) to perceive clearly, by whom would it be grasped?
If there were no grasping, by whom would it be contained? This is how the former leads into the latter. Because there is that which contains, the initial impurity acts as the seed;
thus, the movements of thought and the arising of consciousness—whether seven, six, or five in number—inevitably fall within the limits of birth and extinction. Therefore, it is not [permanent].
It transcends the three objects, the three measures, and the three natures; the karmic consciousness is boundless. This is how the latter penetrates the former.
In essence, when there is a single awakening, then every inch of the nature of consciousness, past and present, is entirely gold, and thus the wondrous mystery of mutual generation is realized.

There are three types of objects (*ālambana*), three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and three types of nature (*svabhāva*). The three types of objects are: the objective realm (*tāttvika-viṣaya*), the realm with a shared substance (*sābhāsa-viṣaya*), and the realm of solitary images (*pratibimba-mātra-viṣaya*).

The three types of valid cognition are: direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*), inference (*anumāna-pramāṇa*), and non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*). The three types of nature are: wholesome (*kuśala-svabhāva*), unwholesome (*akuśala-svabhāva*), and indeterminate (*avyākṛta-svabhāva*).

Direct perception necessarily apprehends the objective realm; inference necessarily apprehends the realm with a shared substance; and non-valid cognition [necessarily apprehends the realm of solitary images].
It is definitively established that there are only solitary images as objects. Regarding "objects by way of nature": these are the objects manifested solely by the mind within the three realms.

Regarding "substance by way of accompaniment": these are objects falsely superimposed upon the illusory body through its provisional combination. Regarding "images by way of solitude": these are like the objects of flowers in a mirror or the moon in water.
By speaking of these three types of objects, all objects—whether mundane or sagely, empty or substantial—are exhausted. By speaking of the three measures (*pramāṇa*),...

All delusions, numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges, regarding views and thoughts are exhausted. Regarding the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), all experiences of cause and effect, suffering and pleasure, are exhausted.
The nature of objective measure (*viṣayapramāṇasvabhāva*) pervades the faculties, objects, and consciousness; therefore, it extends throughout the nine stages, the seven destinies, and all times.
This is truly because, at the very beginning, one becomes deluded regarding the originally existing light of wisdom, whereby a latent knot is formed through a single moment of false perception.
It serves as the seed for maintaining warmth and consciousness. Thus, consciousness relies upon the breath. That which moves through the blowing of the breath is wind;

that which moistens through the blowing of the breath is water; that which exhales heat through the blowing of the breath is fire; and that which coagulates through the blowing of the breath is earth.
Therefore, flesh constitutes the body and the vital energy constitutes life. By gathering these four great elements, the internal body is formed.
It is merely by borrowing the four great elements that one forms a body; in reality, it is a body brought about by the solidification of ignorance.
Thus it is said that form is intermingled with delusive thoughts, and that the characteristics of thought constitute the body.

When the life-root reaches maturity, it is difficult to break free, for life completes consciousness and consciousness completes life, like flour entering oil and oil entering flour, revolving back and forth, ensnared within uninterrupted consciousness.
In meditative concentration (*samādhi*), that consciousness has not yet departed, yet this consciousness arises immediately. Even if it remains pure for a brief moment, it is like a rushing torrent;
because the flow is so swift, it cannot be seen, yet it is not truly non-arising. Since consciousness clings to this as "self," it is naturally easy to enter the gate but difficult to exit.
Unless one encounters old age, sickness, death, or the exhaustion of karmic retribution, how could one ever escape? Even if...
At that time, although one has shed the delusions regarding the nature of consciousness, one still remains as an intermediate state being (*antarābhava*). The suffering of fear is redoubled;
having taken on a body of a different species, the confinement of ignorance becomes even more severe. Thus, one becomes a non-Buddhist adherent of the view of annihilation (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*);
when the kalpa ends, consciousness arises again. Even if one becomes a deity in the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*), when the retribution is exhausted, consciousness sprouts once more.

Generally speaking, because the nature of consciousness possesses the three measures and the three natures, it spontaneously gives rise to the five universal mental factors, the five object-specific mental factors, the six afflictions, and the four indeterminate mental factors.
Such various delusions of the nature of consciousness produce the coarse karma of consciousness.
This cannot escape being the subtle karma of consciousness. Therefore, to clarify the nature of *vijñapti-mātra*, one must undergo a great awakening; only then will one not be deceiving oneself.

Otherwise, one will not fail to cling to the realm of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-viṣaya*), but will certainly cling to the realm of the "concrete-with-essence" (*saviṣaya-sadṛśa-viṣaya*). If one does not cling to this realm, [one has attained it].

When one is fixed upon the object of a solitary reflection, one cannot escape the absence of objects; this is true for the three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).

Likewise, one cannot escape the absence of measures (*māna*) and the absence of nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). How much more so regarding objects, measures, and natures, which are fundamentally forged as a single whole—this makes it all the more difficult for people to achieve transcendence.
For instance, when the eye perceives the colors blue and yellow, this seeing does not require artificial arrangement, yet it is not direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
When one turns a thought and confirms that blue is indeed blue and yellow is indeed yellow, is this not *anumāna* (inference)?

When one turns another thought and, conversely, doubts whether blue is necessarily blue or yellow is necessarily yellow, such that the inferential measurement fails to reach its mark, is this not *an-apramāṇa* (non-measurement)?

Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) belongs to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Inference and the other two [types of] measurement belong to the two natures of wholesome and unwholesome. As for the eyes seeing blue and yellow—

A provisional arrangement is the "nature-object" (*xingjing*); this is because the object and the eye have forgotten each other. When one turns a thought and confirms it as blue or yellow, this is the "object-with-substance" (*daizhijing*);
this is because the object and the eye are joined. When one turns a thought and instead suspects that it may not be blue or yellow, this is the "solitary shadow-object" (*duyingjing*);
this is because the object and the eye are not real. Seeing blue or yellow for the first time is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

Nature (*svabhāva*). When conditions such as blue or yellow arise, attachment is produced; this constitutes the two natures of good and evil. Regarding the three natures, the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and the three objects:

since these apply universally to all phenomena, one knows that when the first five consciousnesses do not engage in conceptual interpretation, they apprehend the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of an object;

this is the "objective nature" (*svabhāvaviṣaya*). When they take a mind or mental factor as their object, they apprehend it as a "nature-bearing object" (*sasvabhāvaviṣaya*). When they take a phenomenon lacking substantial reality as their object, this is the "solitary shadow" (*kevalacchāyāviṣaya*).

The objective field (*viṣaya*) refers to the sixth, the clearly discerning mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). When it encounters the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) that were previously perceived by the first five consciousnesses within a state of sudden, initial attention (*sahaja-citta*), it is an objective field of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-viṣaya*).
When it takes as its object one's own currently functioning mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), it is an objective field with a shared substance (*sadravya-viṣaya*).

When it simultaneously takes as its object the minds and mental factors of another person, it is an objective field of solitary images (*pratibimba-mātra-viṣaya*). By extension, it is not only the objective field that possesses these three types of fields.
The faculties likewise possess three objects, and consciousness likewise possesses three objects; thus, nature arises from measure, and measure arises from objects.

If one awakens to the emptiness of objects, then one views the triple world as empty flowers and regards seeing and hearing as dreams and illusions. Thereby, the nature of consciousness becomes pure, and the purity of the Dharma-eye is attained.
Alas, objects are fundamentally non-existent, yet their arising is caused by the mind; the mind is fundamentally non-existent, yet its arising is caused by objects.
There are. However, when the mind arises, the object arises; when the object arises, the mind arises. Mind and object are mutually dependent and mutually inverted.

Therefore, the external four great elements of the world are the remote *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of my eight consciousnesses, while the internal four great elements of the self-body are the intimate *nimitta-bhāga* of my eight consciousnesses.
Both are produced by the same eight consciousnesses and constitute my common karma.
In the land of retribution where one dwells, only when a single person awakens to the truth and returns to the source can the worlds of the ten directions be extinguished.
Only then can one enter the realm by taking a field of rubble for a lotus boat; only then can one enter the faculties by taking a blood-soaked sack for a diamond cave;
and only then can one enter consciousness by taking a cavern of wandering thoughts for the Land of Fragrant Accumulation.

The general meaning is that delusion and awakening share the same source, and bondage and liberation are non-dual. When the nature of consciousness is once awakened to, the true nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature.
Therefore, do not say that the wisdom of differentiation is difficult to clarify; it is simply that the mind of *nirvāṇa* is difficult to comprehend.

For instance, when the first five consciousnesses are once awakened to, they become the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*). When the sixth consciousness is once awakened to, it becomes the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*). The seventh...
To awaken to the oneness of the *vijñāna* (consciousness) is itself the Wisdom of Equality; to awaken to the oneness of the eight *vijñānas* is itself the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom.

The distinctions between these wisdoms are easy [to understand], but awakening alone is difficult. For if one does not awaken, one’s consciousness will surely remain a vast, wandering stream of karma (*karmavijñāna*), with no fundamental basis to rely upon.

Therefore, it is not a matter of suppression; what is suppressed cannot be true enlightened awareness (*jñāna*). It is not a matter of illumination; what is illuminated cannot be true meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Attainment through meditative concentration is not true insight; understanding through intellectual analysis is not true cultivation or realization. As for one who has realized enlightenment, there is no person to be found—this is a thousandfold and ten-thousandfold difficulty.
Only by means of several verses from Master Xuanzang can one awaken to the meaning beyond the words; perhaps then one may approach it.
A Brief Explanation of the *Eight Consciousnesses’ Rules* (End)
